summary: Proposes using the ACAP configuration protocol to provision wireless phones over the air, which covers activating a device and updating its settings remotely. It is an informational paper rather than a standard, and was replaced by RFC 2636.

eli5.summary: Instead of taking a phone to a shop to set it up, the phone is configured by a message sent through the air. This paper suggests which tool could carry it.

subtitle: Over-the-air provisioning of wireless phones using ACAP.

tldr.problem: Wireless carriers needed to activate and update customer phones remotely without user visits to a shop, reducing costs and improving customer experience.
tldr.mechanism: This document proposes using the ACAP configuration protocol to deliver provisioning and parameter updates to mobile phones over data connections, leveraging existing IS-707 CDMA data services.
tldr.outcome: The approach provides a flexible, extensible platform using open standards that carriers can implement with standard ACAP servers and small client code, allowing both device activation (OTASP) and remote parameter updates (OTAPA).

today: RFC 2636 replaced this document with an updated approach to wireless device provisioning.

sections.title: The Problem: Activating Wireless Phones Remotely
sections.content:
Wireless carriers faced two expensive processes: activating new phones and updating existing ones with new settings or network changes. These tasks typically required customer visits to retail locations or involved complex manual provisioning. The cost and logistics of this system limited how carriers could distribute handsets and serve customers.

This document describes a solution using Over-The-Air Service Provisioning (OTASP) to activate new phones and Over-The-Air Parameter Administration (OTAPA) to update existing phones. By leveraging the data services that carriers were already deploying (IS-707 for CDMA networks), phones can download their activation and configuration data automatically.
sections.eli5: It's hard and expensive for phone companies to set up and update phones manually. This paper shows how to let phones get their instructions from a server in the cloud instead.

sections.title: OTASP and OTAPA Processes
sections.content:
OTASP (Over-The-Air Service Provisioning) allows a new customer to activate a phone without visiting a shop. A customer provides personal and credit information to the carrier (by phone, web form, or in-store kiosk). Once authorized, the customer receives a temporary password, and the phone initiates a data call to the provisioning server. The phone authenticates using the Electronic Serial Number (ESN) and the temporary password, then downloads its Number Assignment Module (NAM), roaming lists, and other parameters.

OTAPA (Over-The-Air Parameter Administration) allows carriers to update provisioning data on active phones remotely. This supports scenarios like area-code splits or firmware updates. OTAPA can be triggered by an SMS notification or by having phones periodically check for changes.
sections.eli5: OTASP is for a brand-new phone getting its first settings. OTAPA is for a phone that's already working, and the company wants to change something on it. Both happen over the air, without the user doing anything.

sections.title: ACAP as the Provisioning Protocol
sections.content:
ACAP (Application Configuration Access Protocol, defined in RFC 2244) is chosen because it is designed precisely for this type of provisioning: it is simple, supports thin clients, works over limited bandwidth, and provides extensible authentication via SASL. The provisioning server is a standard ACAP server running in the carrier's intranet, accepting connections from mobile phones and administrative clients.

Mobile phones authenticate using their ESN and either a shared secret (for previously provisioned phones) or a limited-time password (for new phones). The authentication mechanism is CRAM-MD5 (keyed-MD5 hash), similar to the existing IS-683A method. An A-Key (authentication key) can be generated using a Diffie-Hellman exchange for added security on subsequent sessions.
sections.eli5: ACAP is a protocol perfect for this job: it's designed for phones to grab configuration data from a server. Phones prove they are really phones (not imposters) using a password or secret key.

sections.title: Data Organization and Inheritance
sections.content:
The ACAP server organizes data in an OTAP dataset, with two main trees: provisioning data (prefixed "Provision.") that is downloaded to phones, and client state (prefixed "Client.") where phones store requested information. Records are stored by ESN and NAM (mobile phone number configuration), allowing each phone to have multiple configurations.

ACAP's data inheritance mechanism is powerful: roaming lists, for example, can be stored at a geographic region level and automatically inherited by all phones in that region. If the roaming list changes, administrators update it once, and all phones inherit the new data on their next check-in. This hierarchical structure makes bulk updates efficient.
sections.eli5: The server keeps phone data organized in folders, like how your home computer organizes files. Phones in the same region can inherit settings from a shared folder, so you don't have to update each phone separately.

sections.title: Mobile Client Operations and Session Flow
sections.content:
The mobile ACAP client operates as a state machine. After authenticating with the server, the phone searches for a list of items the server wants information about (like phone manufacturer, model, software version, available memory). The phone responds with this information. Next, it searches for any provisioning data that has changed since the last session, then stores these values in its non-volatile memory.

For OTAPA, phones can be triggered to initiate a session by an SMS notification or by periodically checking in at configured times and days. The check-in interval and schedule are themselves part of the provisioning data, allowing carriers to control when phones synchronize without network-wide coordination.
sections.eli5: When a phone connects, it asks "what do you want to know about me?" The server tells it. Then the phone asks "what's new for me?" and downloads the latest settings. Everything happens in steps, controlled by the server.

sections.title: Security and Future Enhancements
sections.content:
OTASP requires the phone to authenticate to the provisioning server (proving the phone is legitimate). OTAPA requires the phone to validate the server (proving the server is legitimate), preventing attackers from spoofing updates. The ACAP framework supports SASL, which allows stronger authentication mechanisms to be added later as threats evolve.

Since OTASP/OTAPA operates within the carrier's controlled network (IP-based, not over wireless), end-to-end encryption between phone and server could be added as a future enhancement. For now, the provisioning data is transmitted in the clear but protected by authentication and (optionally) network-level encryption like IPSec.
sections.eli5: The phone checks that the server is real before downloading settings. If needed, stronger security can be added later. For now, the carrier's own network is trusted to protect the data.
